d.title: Stripping the markers leaves the structure they were carrying
d.caption: A model trained on text emits text conventions, and a synthesiser has no way to know they were formatting — **emphasis markers become the word "asterisk", a hash becomes "pound", a bullet becomes "dash" or a strange pause.** Nothing warns you; the audio is simply wrong. The instinct is to strip formatting in post-processing, worth doing as a safety net and **the wrong primary fix: a six-item list with the bullets removed is still six items the listener cannot hold.** The real fix is upstream, in the prompt.

nodes.label: Six items are still six items
Fix it upstream, in the prompt

d.title: Eight written forms and how they are actually said
d.caption: **Formatting errors sound wrong and are therefore caught. Numeric errors sometimes sound plausible and change the meaning**, which makes them worse. The worst row is the fourth: *2-3 business days* read as **"two minus three business days"** is not obviously broken audio — it is a sentence, and a listener may simply mishear it. And a reference like `AB-7719` read as "seven thousand" destroys the only thing it was for.

d.title: Five structural rules, all following from working memory
d.caption: A chat answer is written for a reader who can skim, so it front-loads context and offers complete option sets. **A spoken answer is consumed serially by someone holding it in working memory, which is good for about three items** — and every rule follows from that one fact. The last is the one with no workaround: **there is no audio equivalent of indentation**, so a sub-list is simply a flat list with the hierarchy silently lost.

items.label: Answer first, context after
items.sub: the answer is what they are holding; the context is optional

items.label: One or two sentences
items.sub: silence invites the user to speak, which is how conversation works

items.label: One question, never three
items.sub: three questions get one answer, to whichever they remember

items.label: Three items, signposted
items.sub: 'there are three options' gives the listener a frame to fill

items.label: No nested structure at all
items.sub: no audio equivalent of indentation - the hierarchy is lost

d.title: Four ways to reduce recognition errors, in order of value
d.caption: **Contextual biasing is the highest-value one and the cheapest**: supply the recogniser with the terms expected on *this* call — the caller's own contacts, the product names, the payee list — and the rare words that fail stop failing. 5.8 and 6.7 made the same point for retrieval and decoding: **the information is available at request time and costs nothing to supply.** The other three are fallbacks for when you cannot enumerate the vocabulary in advance.

items.label: Contextual biasing
items.sub: supply this call's expected terms - highest value, lowest cost

items.label: Constrained slots
items.sub: decode against the shape you know the answer has

items.label: N-best rescoring
items.sub: take the top several hypotheses and rescore against context

items.label: Phonetic matching
items.sub: match by sound rather than spelling, against a known set

d.title: Confirm on consequence, not on confidence
d.caption: "Confirm when confidence is low" sounds principled and **is the wrong axis**, for two reasons: confidence is poorly calibrated on exactly the rare words that fail — a recogniser can be **confidently wrong about a name it has never seen** — and confidence says nothing about whether being wrong matters. **The column that decides is consequence**, and the error-prone column only refines it. Note row five: an account number spoken as digits is *reliable* and *consequential*, so it gets a cheap check digit rather than a readback.

cells.text: a check digit, not a readback

d.title: A voice agent has one way to represent a pause, and it already means several things
d.caption: A chat agent can show a spinner or three animated dots — all of which say *work in progress* without saying anything. **A voice agent has silence, and silence already has other meanings.** The expensive band is 1.2 to 2 seconds, because **the repeat arrives while your response is being prepared**: it hits the pipeline mid-generation, triggers barge-in if you have it and corrupts the turn if you do not, so you are now handling an interruption on a turn that was merely slow.

d.title: The natural-sounding fillers are the unsafe ones
d.caption: A filler is spoken **before the tool has returned**, so it cannot reference the outcome. This sounds obvious and is violated constantly, because **the natural-sounding phrases are exactly the ones that presume success.** *"Sure, I can do that"* promises success before the tool ran; *"I've cancelled that for you"* states a completed action that may fail; *"Good news!"* promises an outcome it cannot know. The safe set all share one property: they commit to nothing.

d.title: A diagram shows the states; a table lets you assert things about them
d.caption: This is the argument of the whole lesson. **A diagram shows states and edges, so it can reveal a missing state or an edge pointing somewhere odd** — and it cannot tell you that one event is unhandled in one state, because an absent edge looks like a deliberate omission. **Writing the machine as a table makes that assertable in four lines**, which turns 13.6's behavioural bug into a unit test rather than an incident report.

nodes.label: A diagram of states and edges

d.title: 950 of 1,000 turns are interrupted while the agent is not speaking
d.caption: It is easy to assume interruption only matters while the agent is talking — **that is what the word suggests**. But most of the turn is spent elsewhere, and an interruption during THINKING needs different handling: **there is no audio to stop and no buffer to flush, but there is generation to cancel** and a tool call that may already be in flight. A state machine written around SPEAKING alone handles the loud case and drops the common one.

d.title: The crash and the defect are nowhere near each other
d.caption: Replaying a realistic event sequence through both versions is the instructive part. **The buggy machine handles the interruption without complaint, loses history correctness silently, and then breaks four steps later on an event nobody considered** — so the crash and the defect are separated by four turns, which is exactly the distance that makes a bug hard to find. The structural fix beyond catching bugs: **each state has invariants you can assert on entry**, and one assertion per state catches a leaked generation task or an unflushed buffer immediately.

nodes.label: Crash and defect are four turns apart
Assert each state's invariants on entry

d.title: Four layers, and only one of them a text harness can reach
d.caption: **Recognition needs audio by definition. Interaction needs timing, and a text eval has none. Experience needs audio to rate.** Only the task layer is reachable — and a text eval measures it **on an input the user never produced**, so it is the one layer that is both reachable and misleading. 13.9 measured why the recognition target is entity error rate rather than WER: **10.6% WER hiding a 41.2% entity error rate** on the same transcripts, so a gate watching WER passes releases that break names and numbers.

cells.text: no - a text eval has no timing
yes - and on an input nobody spoke

d.title: Four turns, four different problems, zero spread
d.caption: The case for per-stage spans is usually made abstractly — *more detail is better, you can drill down*. The concrete version finishes the argument: **four turns that differ in what is wrong with them and are identical in total duration.** One is healthy, one has a patient endpointer, one was interrupted, one has a recogniser struggling. **The spread across all four is 0 ms**, so the metric most dashboards carry cannot distinguish a healthy turn from three broken ones.

d.title: Six spans, and the attribute pair only voice needs
d.caption: Each attribute earns its place by distinguishing one of §01's four turns. **The endpoint threshold because it is the largest term in the budget and a config value nobody remembers.** The ASR partial count because **a high count means the recogniser kept revising**, which correlates with a hard utterance. And the last row is the pair no text system has: **words generated against words played**, which is the only way to see 13.6's phantom-context bug in the data.

d.title: The most common voice instrumentation error
d.caption: **Every figure in this module is measured from the moment the user stopped speaking**, and the most common instrumentation error is to start the clock at the endpointer instead. A dashboard measuring from there shows a healthy median **and, crucially, shows no endpointing span at all** — so the 42.4% of the budget that 13.3 identified as the largest single lever is invisible in the data, and every optimisation discussion is about the remaining 58%.

d.title: Five artefacts, five retentions, decided by what each contains
d.caption: The policy falls out of the content. **Span timings carry no PII, so keep them 90 days — this is the debugging substrate.** The redacted transcript is enough to reconstruct a turn's shape at 30 days. Raw transcripts contain everything the caller said, so 7. And audio is the only artefact that **reproduces a recognition bug**, which is why a consent-gated rolling window exists at all — and why 13.12's eval set has to be a separate, explicitly consented collection.

d.title: Three unrelated meters, and the ranking is counter-intuitive
d.caption: A cascaded call bills in three units with nothing to do with each other: recognition **per minute of audio**, synthesis **per character of text**, the model **per token** with input and output priced apart. **Three unrelated meters is why intuition about which dominates is usually wrong** — and the measured ranking is TTS, then the model, then ASR. **Synthesis is 39.6% of the call and 16.9% larger than the model**, which inverts where a team's cost attention naturally goes.

d.title: 87.9% off the input line, for a configuration change
d.caption: **Most of each turn's prompt is byte-identical to the previous turn's**: the system prompt never changes, and the conversation history up to the last exchange is exactly what was sent before. Caching those reads at a fraction of the input price takes input cost from **$0.03157 to $0.00383 — 87.9%** — and cuts the fastest-growing line in a voice call **without changing a single behaviour**, which is the rarest property any lever in this course has.

d.title: Six levers, and the only one that trades quality
d.caption: **The two largest are a prompt rewrite and a caching flag, worth 59.4% of the call between them**, and neither changes the model, the architecture or the vendor. Together they are worth more than moving to a cheaper model would be — and they carry **no quality risk**, where a smaller model is **the one lever in the whole module that trades it.** Note that writing for the ear cuts latency as well, so it appears twice in this course's ledger.

cells.text: none - and it cuts latency too

d.title: The environment is a parameter, and nobody lists it
d.caption: **Every number in this module — the 1,650 ms budget, the 700 ms endpointer, the 60 ms playout buffer, the 160 ms barge-in — was measured on a laptop with a good network and headphones.** That is not a criticism of the numbers; it is the observation that the environment is a parameter. Telephony adds 210 ms and a connected car adds **380 ms before any code changes**, and the right-hand column shows every target is improvable — but the ordering never changes, so the easiest case stays easiest.

d.title: The requirement that drives the architecture is the tunnel
d.caption: A car is the worst listening environment in normal use — road noise rising with speed, HVAC, wind, passengers, music, and a microphone some distance from the speaker's mouth. Mic arrays and beamforming help, and speaker identification matters. **But the requirement that actually drives the architecture is different: it has to work in a tunnel.** An assistant that stops functioning when connectivity drops is not acceptable in a car, **and that cannot be fixed with a retry** — it forces a local model, which changes every number in the budget.

nodes.label: But it has to work in a tunnel

d.caption: The list closes the module because every row has a number attached rather than a warning. **Fixed silence endpointing leaves 42.4% of the budget untouched. Evaluating on typed text reports 100% where the real figure is 38%. Ignoring entity error rate hides a 41.2% figure behind a 10.6% WER.** And two rows are structural rather than costly: no echo cancellation produces the stuttering demo, and a deep jitter buffer makes barge-in unreachable by construction.
